faq.heading: Questions about {productName}

items.a: {productName} is local-first restaurant inventory and food-cost software for independent restaurants.
No. Detection creates a reviewable draft. The restaurant reviews, corrects, and explicitly posts the purchase.

items.q: Can it track supplier price changes?
items.a: The launch release compares current and previous prices using normalized base-unit cost and retains the source purchase line. If package conversion data is insufficient, it shows that the comparison is incomplete.

items.q: Can it calculate preparation and menu-item cost?
items.a: The launch release covers preparation batch and yield cost, plus menu plate cost, food-cost percentage, and gross profit before labor and overhead.

items.q: What happens when costs are missing?
items.a: The product labels cost coverage as Complete, Partial, or Missing costs. It does not invent precision when source costs are unavailable.
The launch release includes count units, numeric entry, progress and resume, variance review, and explicit posting. Zero remains different from uncounted.
Yes. It identifies below-par ingredients and prepares a supplier-grouped, package-aware shopping list. The initial release does not electronically place supplier orders.

items.q: Does it connect to POS or accounting systems?
items.a: Not in the first release. No integration date is being promised.

items.q: What platform is the initial release?
items.a: Android. The product is local-first; Web, iOS, and cloud sync are not first-release availability claims.

items.q: Is it designed for multi-location chains?
items.a: The initial focus is one restaurant and one location, not enterprise multi-location management.

restaurantInventory.seoTitle: Restaurant Inventory Information in One Place | {productName} by Venkoi
restaurantInventory.seoDescription: Learn why restaurant inventory becomes difficult when information lives in different places and how to bring it together.
restaurantInventory.title: Inventory gets harder when the information lives in different places.
restaurantInventory.description: Why keeping inventory, purchases, and costs in separate places makes restaurant operations more difficult than they need to be.

content.intro: Managing a restaurant kitchen is already complicated. Keeping track of the products that make the kitchen run shouldn't add unnecessary weight to the day.
content.problemTitle: The problem is not simply counting inventory.
content.problemBody: Inventory is often treated as a standalone task—a weekly count of what is on the shelf. But in a real operation, that number doesn't exist in a vacuum. It is the result of everything that happened since the last count.
content.purchasesTitle: Purchases tell only part of the story
content.purchasesBody: Knowing what you bought is essential for paying vendors, but without connecting those purchases to what you already have, you only see what came in, not what is actually available for use.
content.quantitiesBody: A count of '24 cases' is just a number. It becomes information when you know how many you started with, how many you received, and how many you expected to have left.
content.activityBody: Between receiving a delivery and taking the next count, product movement occurs. When this activity is tracked separately from the inventory count, it's harder to understand why your numbers changed.
content.costsTitle: Costs make the picture more useful
content.costsBody: Inventory represents a significant investment. When cost information lives in an invoice folder or a separate spreadsheet, it's harder to see the cost history of what is on your shelves and how price changes may be affecting the operation.
content.togetherTitle: Why bringing the information together matters
content.togetherBody: When purchasing, inventory counts, activity, and costs are part of the same picture, the information becomes more useful. It helps remove guesswork and provides a clearer view of where resources are going.
content.zaikoBody: {productName} is designed to bring these four areas—inventory, purchases, activity, and costs—into a single, focused experience. It focuses on providing clearer visibility into your operation without adding unnecessary complexity.

restaurantInventoryCounts.seoTitle: Restaurant Inventory Counts: Zero, Uncounted, and Variance | Venkoi
restaurantInventoryCounts.seoDescription: Learn how expected inventory, physical counts, count units, variance review, and traceable adjustments fit together.
restaurantInventoryCounts.title: Restaurant inventory counts: zero, uncounted, and variance
restaurantInventoryCounts.description: A practical guide to recording what was found, separating zero from unfinished work, and reviewing variance before inventory changes.

content.intro: A physical count is where the inventory record meets the shelf. The result is trustworthy only when the count preserves what someone actually found, what they have not checked yet, and what the restaurant reviewed before posting an adjustment.
content.expectedTitle: Expected inventory is a reference, not the count
content.expectedBody: Expected inventory may be calculated from the previous balance and the activity recorded since then: purchases, usage, waste, transfers, or earlier adjustments. It gives the person counting a point of comparison. It does not prove what is physically present.
content.expectedBody2: Counted quantity is different. It is the amount someone actually finds during the physical count. Keeping expected and counted quantities separate makes variance visible instead of allowing the system's estimate to replace an observation.
content.statesTitle: Zero and uncounted are different states
content.statesBody: 0 means counted and found zero. Uncounted means not counted yet. If both states are stored as zero, an unfinished count can look like a confirmed empty shelf and create an incorrect adjustment.
content.statesExample: Fictional example: tomatoes are expected at 8 cases and counted at 0 cases, so their status is Counted. Chicken breast is expected at 12 packs but has no entry, so its status is Uncounted. The tomatoes may require review; the chicken still requires a count.
content.unitsBody: Restaurants receive, store, and count products in different units: case, bag, bottle, each, pound, or ounce. A person may count two cases while inventory is maintained in pounds. That conversion is useful only when the package and unit relationship is known.
content.unitsBody2: Conversions should be understandable and reviewable. Some products do not have enough information for a reliable conversion, and variable-weight products may not fit a fixed assumption. In those cases, the gap should remain visible instead of being hidden behind a precise-looking number.
content.progressTitle: Progress matters when a count takes time
content.progressBody: A full count rarely happens in one uninterrupted pass. The team needs to see what has been counted, what remains, where work stopped, and which entries need review. Saving progress also prevents a resumed count from turning blank items into accidental zeros.
content.varianceTitle: Variance is expected compared with counted
content.varianceBody: Variance is the difference between the expected quantity and the counted quantity. It is an operational signal, not an explanation by itself. A difference may point to missing activity, a unit error, spoilage, portioning, theft, or a simple counting mistake.
content.varianceBody2: Large or surprising differences deserve review. Check the count entry, unit, recent purchases, waste, and other recorded activity before deciding that the inventory record should change.
content.reviewTitle: Review first, then post the adjustment
content.reviewBody: A completed count should not silently rewrite inventory. The restaurant should review the variance and explicitly post the approved adjustment. That moment separates observation from the decision to change the official quantity.
content.traceTitle: Keep the adjustment connected to the count
content.traceBody: After posting, the adjustment should remain linked to the physical-count event. Later, an operator can see what changed, where it came from, when it happened, and which operational action caused it. History is a trust layer, not just a log.

They include reviewable numeric counts, visible units and conversions, saved progress, and explicit adjustment posting, with limitations shown when conversion information is insufficient.

restaurantFoodCost.seoTitle: Restaurant Food Cost: From Ingredient Cost to Menu Item | Venkoi
restaurantFoodCost.seoDescription: Understand how supplier package costs flow through ingredients, preparations, yield, menu items, and food-cost coverage.
restaurantFoodCost.title: Restaurant food cost: from ingredient cost to menu item
restaurantFoodCost.description: How package prices become usable ingredient costs, flow through preparations and yield, and reach the cost of a plate.

content.intro: Food cost is a chain of connected calculations. Each result depends on the source information before it. Following that chain makes the number explainable and makes missing information visible.
content.packageBody: The price on a purchase usually belongs to a package: a case, bag, bottle, or box. That total is important for the purchase record, but it may not be the unit used in a recipe. A $24 case is not yet a cost per pound unless the case weight is known.
content.normalizedTitle: Normalize cost only when the conversion is known
content.normalizedBody: With sufficient package information, the purchase cost can be converted to a useful base unit. For example, a fictional 12-pound case purchased for $24 costs $2 per pound. The arithmetic is simple; the reliability depends on the package actually containing 12 pounds.
content.normalizedBody2: Not every package has a complete or fixed conversion. If weight, quantity, or another required relationship is missing, the system should not guess a base-unit cost.
content.preparationTitle: Preparations carry ingredient cost into a batch
content.preparationBody: Restaurants turn ingredients into sauces, stocks, dressings, dough, and other prepared components. The preparation's batch cost comes from its ingredients. To make that cost useful for recipes, the restaurant also needs the batch quantity and usable yield.
content.yieldBody: Suppose a fictional tomato-sauce batch uses $8 of tomatoes, $2 of oil, and $1 of seasoning. The batch costs $11. If it produces 22 usable portions, each portion costs $0.50. If the actual yield changes, the cost per portion changes even when ingredient prices stay the same.
content.menuTitle: A plate can combine ingredients and preparations
content.menuBody: A menu item's cost may include direct ingredients, measured portions of preparations, and other components. Each component should bring its own supported cost into the plate calculation. This creates a path back from the menu-item total to the purchases and conversions behind it.
content.percentageTitle: Food-cost percentage is one relationship, not the whole business
content.percentageBody: Food-cost percentage compares plate cost with selling price: plate cost divided by selling price. The result can help an operator review pricing and portions, but no single percentage is universally right for every restaurant or menu item.
content.percentageBody2: Selling price minus plate cost shows gross profit before labor and overhead. Gross profit is not net profit. Rent, payroll, utilities, fees, waste, and other expenses still matter.
content.coverageTitle: Missing source costs must stay visible
content.coverageBody: If an ingredient has no supported cost, any preparation or menu item that depends on it is incomplete. Cost coverage can be described as Complete, Partial, or Missing costs. If source costs are missing, show the gap instead of inventing precision.

productAvailability.available: {productName} connects supplier purchase cost to ingredient cost, preparation and batch cost, yield, and menu-item cost. It presents food-cost percentage, gross profit before labor and overhead, and cost coverage while keeping source gaps visible.
productAvailability.early-access: Some of these connected costing workflows are currently available to participating restaurants. They connect supported source costs through ingredients, preparations, yield, and menu items while keeping missing-cost coverage visible.
productAvailability.launch-release: For the initial release, {productName} is planned to connect supplier purchase cost to ingredient cost, preparation and batch cost, yield, and menu-item cost. It is planned to show food-cost percentage, gross profit before labor and overhead, and cost coverage while keeping source gaps visible.

restaurantSupplierPrices.seoTitle: How to Track Restaurant Supplier Price Changes | Venkoi
restaurantSupplierPrices.seoDescription: Learn how package size, unit conversion, comparable purchases, and source context make supplier price changes meaningful.
restaurantSupplierPrices.title: Track supplier price changes without comparing the wrong things
restaurantSupplierPrices.description: Why package totals can mislead, how normalized unit costs help, and when a price comparison should remain incomplete.

content.intro: A higher invoice line does not always mean the ingredient became more expensive. Before comparing two purchases, the restaurant needs to know whether the packages represent the same usable quantity.
content.problemTitle: Package prices are not automatically comparable
content.problemBody: A 12-unit case and a 24-unit case are different purchasing units. The same is true for a 5-pound bag and a 10-pound bag. The larger package can cost more in total while costing less for each usable unit.
content.exampleTitle: Compare the package and the unit
content.exampleBody: Fictional example: Purchase A is a 12-unit case for $24, or $2 per unit. Purchase B is a 24-unit case for $42, or $1.75 per unit. The package price increased by $18, or 75%, while the unit price decreased by $0.25, or 12.5%. Looking only at $24 to $42 would give the wrong operational signal.
content.comparableBody: The latest purchase should be compared with a previous purchase that can be expressed in the same base unit. That may require a known package size and unit conversion. Supplier, product identity, and packaging context also matter; the immediately previous invoice line is not always the right comparison.
content.incompleteBody: Sometimes the information needed to normalize two packages is missing or unreliable. A variable-weight case may lack its actual weight, or a package quantity may never have been recorded. In that situation, a trustworthy system should mark the comparison incomplete instead of calculating a confident percentage from incompatible totals.
content.changesTitle: Show both absolute and percentage change
content.changesBody: Once two base-unit costs are comparable, absolute change shows the amount added or removed per unit. Percentage change shows that difference relative to the earlier cost. Both should be tied to the units being compared so the number cannot be mistaken for a package-level change.
content.sourceTitle: Keep the number connected to its source
content.sourceBody: An operator reviewing a change should be able to see the supplier, package, purchase date, source purchase line, and previous comparable purchase. That context makes price history verifiable and helps reveal a packaging change or data-entry issue.

productAvailability.available: {productName} connects the latest comparable price with the previous comparable price, shows absolute and percentage changes, and preserves package price, normalized cost, source purchase context, and supplier history. Insufficient conversion information leaves the comparison incomplete. It does not negotiate with suppliers or electronically place orders.
productAvailability.early-access: Some supplier-price workflows are currently available to participating restaurants, including supported comparable prices and source purchase context. Insufficient conversion information leaves the comparison incomplete. The product does not negotiate with suppliers or electronically place orders.
productAvailability.launch-release: The initial release of {productName} is planned to connect comparable supplier prices, show absolute and percentage changes, and preserve package price, normalized cost, source purchase context, and supplier history. Insufficient conversion information will leave the comparison incomplete. It will not negotiate with suppliers or electronically place orders.

startSoftwareProject.seoTitle: How to Start a Software Project Without a Finished Specification | Venkoi
startSoftwareProject.seoDescription: You don't need a finished software specification to get started. Learn what information helps kick off a successful project with Venkoi.
startSoftwareProject.title: You don't need a finished software specification to get started.
startSoftwareProject.description: Why bringing a problem, goal, or workflow is more important than arriving with a technical document.

content.intro: One of the most common reasons software projects never get off the ground is the belief that you need a perfect technical plan before you even speak to a developer.
content.problemTitle: Start with the problem or goal
content.problemBody: At Venkoi, we believe the best software starts with a clear understanding of what you want to accomplish. You don't need to know the database structure; you need to know why the software needs to exist.
content.usersTitle: Know who the experience is for
content.usersBody: Understanding who will use the software is more valuable than knowing which programming language will be used. Knowing the users helps shape an experience that actually solves their problems.
content.workflowBody: What is the one thing the user must be able to do successfully? If you can describe that process, you have enough to start a conversation.
content.existingBody: Whether it's a stack of paper forms, a complicated spreadsheet, or an aging piece of software, showing how the process works today gives us the best starting point for improvement.
content.prioritiesTitle: Separate what matters now from what can come later
content.prioritiesBody: You don't need every feature on day one. Bringing an idea of what is essential for the first version allows us to focus on delivering value quickly.
content.processTitle: From idea to design, development and testing
content.processBody: Our four-stage lifecycle—Idea & Direction, Design, Development, and Testing & Quality—is designed to take your goal and turn it into a high-quality product, even if you don't have the technical details figured out yet.

websiteOrWebApp.seoTitle: Website or Web Application? How to Choose | Venkoi
websiteOrWebApp.seoDescription: Understand the difference between a website and a web application and how to choose the right approach for your project.
websiteOrWebApp.title: Website or web application? Start with what you want people to accomplish.
websiteOrWebApp.description: How to decide between a content-focused website and an interactive web application based on your goals.

content.intro: The terms 'website' and 'web application' are often used interchangeably, but the distinction matters when deciding how to build your next project.
content.websiteTitle: A website is often centered on communication
content.websiteBody: A website primarily helps people understand your business, discover information, and explore your services. Its main goal is to deliver structured content to the visitor.
content.webappTitle: A web application is often centered on interaction
content.webappBody: A web application involves ongoing interaction, working with changing information, and performing repeat tasks. It's built to handle application state and complex workflows.
content.betweenTitle: Many projects sit somewhere in between
content.betweenBody: The line isn't always sharp. A project might have informational content (website) combined with interactive tools (web application). The architecture should follow what the users need to do.
content.questionsTitle: Questions that help define the right approach
content.questionsBody: Do users need to log in? Are they creating or managing data? Is the content the same for everyone? The answers to these questions help us determine if a website or a web application is the right fit.
content.outcomeTitle: Start with the outcome, not the label
content.outcomeBody: Don't worry about the technical category. Focus on what you want people to accomplish, and we'll help you choose the architecture that makes it possible.
content.cta: Tell us about your web project

privacyPage.seoDescription: Learn how Venkoi LLC collects, uses, shares, and retains information on the Venkoi marketing website.
privacyPage.title: Privacy Policy
privacyPage.introduction: This Privacy Policy explains how Venkoi LLC handles information through the Venkoi marketing website, Contact and Demo forms, and current free-offer interest flow. It does not govern a future authenticated Venkoi or {productName} software product.

sections.title: Who operates this website
paragraphs: Venkoi LLC operates https://venkoi.com. In this policy, “Venkoi,” “we,” “us,” and “our” refer to Venkoi LLC.

sections.title: Information you provide
paragraphs: Depending on the form and information you choose to submit, we collect the following categories:
bullets: Name, or first and last name; email address; optional phone number; and company or business name.
Restaurant location count and information about the inventory tools or systems currently used.
Service interest, project stage, message, Demo or product interest, and free-offer interest.
The selected website language, source path, permitted UTM attribution fields, and a normalized external referrer when available.

sections.title: Technical information and website tools
paragraphs: Normal browser, device, network, request, and security information may be processed as needed to deliver and protect the website. Vercel provides hosting and request processing, privacy-oriented Web Analytics, Speed Insights performance measurement, and BotID anti-abuse verification.

Venkoi’s current application does not create cookies or localStorage tracking, build fingerprint-based customer profiles, preserve attribution across browser sessions, or track a visitor’s journey across pages. Infrastructure and security providers may still process technical browser, device, or network signals as part of their services.

sections.title: How we use information
bullets: Respond to Contact requests and communicate about a submitted request.
Handle Demo requests and free-offer interest.
Operate, secure, troubleshoot, and improve the website.
Understand aggregated website usage and performance.
Prevent fraud, spam, automated abuse, and bots.
Maintain business records during the approved retention period.

sections.title: Service providers
paragraphs: We use service providers that support our operations: Vercel for hosting, platform functionality, analytics, performance measurement, and BotID; Neon for database persistence; and Resend for transactional email delivery. These providers process information to support the services they provide to Venkoi. We do not sell lead information to them.

sections.title: Emails
paragraphs: A Contact, Demo, or free-offer submission may result in transactional or direct-response email related to that request. Submitting a form does not enroll you in an unrelated marketing newsletter. Venkoi does not currently operate a marketing mailing list through these forms.

sections.title: Sale and targeted advertising
paragraphs: Venkoi does not currently sell personal information. Venkoi does not currently use submitted lead information for third-party targeted advertising.

sections.title: Retention
paragraphs: Unconverted Contact, Demo, and free-offer lead records are ordinarily retained for up to 24 months from the last meaningful interaction, then deleted or anonymized unless a legitimate legal, security, dispute, or ongoing-business reason requires longer retention. If a lead becomes a customer, its information may later be subject to a different customer or business-record retention policy.

This retention rule is an operational policy. Automated deletion or anonymization is not yet implemented, and Venkoi must carry out the required review and deletion or anonymization process operationally.

sections.title: Privacy requests
paragraphs: To ask about Venkoi’s privacy practices or request access to, correction of, or deletion of information we maintain about you, email {privacyEmail}. Requests are handled where applicable. We may need to verify your identity before disclosing, changing, or deleting personal information.

sections.title: California and online privacy disclosures
paragraphs: The categories collected are described above and include identifiers and contact, business, request, attribution, and technical information. We disclose information to the service-provider categories described above to operate the website and respond to requests. You may use {privacyEmail} to request review, correction, or deletion where offered.

The application does not currently respond differently to browser Do Not Track or similar preference signals. Venkoi does not use submitted lead information for cross-site targeted advertising, and the application does not authorize other parties to collect personally identifiable information about your activities over time and across unrelated websites for Venkoi advertising. Platform and security providers may process technical signals to provide their services.

sections.title: Changes to this policy
paragraphs: We may update this policy as our website or practices change. Material changes will be communicated by posting the revised policy here with a new effective or updated date. Review this page periodically for the current version.

sections.title: Contact
paragraphs: Privacy questions and requests may be sent to {privacyEmail}.
